prompt: In the name 3-octyne, what does the number 3 tell you?

choices.text: The triple bond starts at C3, so it joins C3 and C4
There are three triple bonds in the chain
choices.why: More than one triple bond is shown by the suffix (diyne, triyne). The number gives the position of the first alkyne carbon.

choices.text: The triple bond joins C2 and C3
choices.why: The locant is the number of the first alkyne carbon. A triple bond between C2 and C3 would make the compound 2-octyne.

choices.text: There is a methyl group on C3
choices.why: A substituent's number goes right before its own name, as in 6-methyl. The number in front of -octyne locates the triple bond.

explanation: Alkynes take the suffix -yne, and the position of the triple bond is shown by the number of the first alkyne carbon in the chain. In 3-octyne (oct-3-yne in the newer system), the triple bond runs from C3 to C4 of an eight-carbon chain, numbered from the end nearer the triple bond.

prompt: What is the IUPAC name of CH3CH2C≡CCH2CH(CH3)CH2CH3?

choices.why: Numbered from the wrong end. Numbering begins at the end nearer the triple bond, which gives the triple bond 3 rather than 5.
This chain stops short. The longest chain runs on through the ethyl group, giving eight carbons with a methyl branch.
The locant is the number of the first alkyne carbon. Numbered from the left, the triple bond joins C3 and C4, so it gets 3.

explanation: The longest chain containing the triple bond has eight carbons, so the parent is an octyne. Numbering starts from the end nearer the triple bond (the left end here), putting the triple bond at C3 and the methyl group at C6: 6-methyl-3-octyne, or 6-methyloct-3-yne in the newer system. This is the section's first example.

prompt: What is the IUPAC name of (CH3)2CHC≡CCH(CH3)2?

choices.why: The parent must be the longest chain containing the triple bond. Running from one methyl group through to the other gives six carbons, not four.
The -ene suffix is for a double bond. A triple bond takes the suffix -yne.
The locant is the number of the first alkyne carbon, and that is C3 from either end. The triple bond joins C3 and C4.

explanation: The longest chain runs from one methyl group through the triple bond to a methyl group on the other side: six carbons, a hexyne. The molecule is symmetrical, so either end gives the triple bond the number 3 and puts methyl groups on C2 and C5: 2,5-dimethyl-3-hexyne (Exercise 9.1.1a).

prompt: What is the IUPAC name of CH3CH2C(CH3)2C≡CCH2CH2CH3?

choices.why: The triple bond gets 4 from either end, so the tie is broken by the branches: start at the end nearer the first branch point, which gives 3,3.
This seven-carbon chain leaves the ethyl group as a branch. The longest chain runs through the ethyl group and has eight carbons.
Each methyl needs its own number, even when both are on the same carbon, so the name needs two locants: 3,3.

explanation: The longest chain has eight carbons, and the triple bond joins C4 and C5 counting from either end. When the triple bond is the same distance from both ends, the alkene rule this section builds on (Section 7.3) says to begin at the end nearer the first branch point. That puts both methyls on C3: 3,3-dimethyl-4-octyne (Exercise 9.1.1c).

prompt: What is the IUPAC name of (CH3)2CHC≡CC(CH3)2CH2CH3?

choices.why: Numbered from the wrong end. From the left the triple bond starts at C3; from the right it would start at C4.
The ethyl group belongs in the main chain. Running through it gives seven carbons, not six.
A triple bond takes the suffix -yne, not -ene.

explanation: The longest chain runs from the isopropyl end, through the triple bond, and along the ethyl group: seven carbons, a heptyne. Numbering from the left, the end nearer the triple bond, gives the triple bond the number 3 and methyl groups on C2, C5 and C5: 2,5,5-trimethyl-3-heptyne (Exercise 9.1.1d).

prompt: What is the IUPAC name of HC≡CCH2CH(CH3)CH2CH2CH=CHCH3?

choices.why: Double bonds get the lower number only when there is a choice. Here the left end reaches a multiple bond first (C1 versus C2), so numbering starts there.
Compounds with both double and triple bonds are named as enynes, not ynenes: the -en part comes before -yne.
A diyne has two triple bonds. This chain has one triple bond and one double bond, so it is an enyne.

explanation: The nine-carbon chain contains a triple and a double bond, so it is an enyne. Numbering starts from the end nearer the first multiple bond, whether double or triple. From the left the triple bond starts at C1; from the right the double bond would start at C2. So the triple bond is at C1, the methyl at C4 and the double bond at C7: 4-methyl-7-nonen-1-yne (4-methylnon-7-en-1-yne in the newer system), one of the section's examples.

prompt: What is the IUPAC name of H2C=CHCH2CH2CH2C≡CH?

choices.why: Each end reaches a multiple bond at C1, so there is a choice. When there is a choice, double bonds receive lower numbers than triple bonds.
Compounds with both double and triple bonds are named as enynes, not ynenes.
A diyne has two triple bonds. This chain has one double bond and one triple bond.

explanation: Numbering an enyne chain starts from the end nearer the first multiple bond. Here both ends have a multiple bond at C1, so the tie-breaker applies: double bonds receive lower numbers than triple bonds. The name is 1-hepten-6-yne (hept-1-en-6-yne in the newer system), the section's example.

prompt: In the IUPAC name of CH3CH=CHCH=CHC≡CCH3, what number does the triple bond receive?
explanation: From either end of the eight-carbon chain, the first multiple bond starts at C2: a double bond from the left, the triple bond from the right. With a choice like this, double bonds receive the lower numbers, so numbering starts at the left. The double bonds are at C2 and C4 and the triple bond at C6 (Exercise 9.1.1e).

prompt: What is the CH3CH2C≡C– substituent called?

choices.why: Butyl, CH3CH2CH2CH2–, is the alkyl group, with no multiple bond.
1-Butenyl, CH3CH2CH=CH–, has a double bond. A triple bond makes this an alkynyl group.
3-Butynyl would be HC≡CCH2CH2–, with the triple bond at the far end. Here the triple bond starts at the attachment carbon, C1.

explanation: Just as alkanes and alkenes give alkyl and alkenyl substituents, alkynes give alkynyl groups. The section's example is CH3CH2C≡C–, 1-butynyl (but-1-ynyl), shown next to butyl and 1-butenyl.
